### The House at the End of Winter

At the end of a street where the chimneys leaned toward one another, there stood a house that had forgotten how to be spring.

Its windows were frosted even in July. Snow rested in the cracks of its roof, though the roof itself was patched with red tiles. A brass plaque beside the door read:

**THE HOUSE AT THE END OF WINTER**  
**Open by appointment.**

Mara had lived across the street her entire life, but she had never seen anyone enter. Her mother said the house belonged to an old woman who collected seasons the way other people collected stamps. When the last snow of winter melted, the old woman moved the house farther down the street, and when autumn came, she moved it back again.

For years, nothing happened.

Then, one November morning, a boy knocked on Mara’s door.

He had pale hair, wet shoes, and the expression of someone who had walked a very long way without being sure where he was going.

“Does the house at the end of winter still exist?” he asked.

“It’s directly across the street,” Mara said.

He looked at the empty space where she was standing, then at the house opposite. Even from there, frost glittered around its windows.

“Could you take me there?”

Mara almost said no. Instead, she found her coat and followed him.

The boy’s name was Elias. He had been apprenticing at a clockmaker’s shop and, on the final day of his apprenticeship, discovered that the oldest clock in the workshop was missing a minute.

Not one of its hands had broken. The clock simply had never received that minute.

“One minute?” Mara asked.

Elias nodded. “My master says it was the minute when winter ends.”

They reached the house. Mara had never noticed a path to its door before, but now there was one, lined with thin blue ice that chimed beneath their shoes. The brass plaque had changed:

**THE HOUSE AT THE END OF WINTER**  
**Please come in. We have been waiting for the missing minute.**

Inside was warmer than expected.

A narrow hallway opened into a room filled with winter. Snow drifted behind the windows without falling. Fireplace logs hissed and popped, though no fire burned. On a table lay the missing clock, its hands moving backward.

An old woman sat beside it.

She looked as though she had been keeping the same expression for a hundred years.

“You have brought the minute,” she said.

“We haven’t,” Mara replied. “We came looking for it.”

The old woman smiled. “That is how it is found.”

She rose and pointed to the clock.

“Every year, the world receives a minute in which winter ends. Often it is only a moment: a thaw in the air, a softened edge of ice, one bright minute somewhere in the long grey. But this year, the minute was lost before it could arrive.”

Elias looked frightened. “What happens if it never comes?”

“Then winter remains.”

Outside, Mara heard the wind sharpen. Frost spread across the windows, racing along the glass.

The old woman opened a small wooden box. Inside was a glass vial no larger than her thumb, filled with a trembling drop of water.

“This is the last piece of the spring we had,” she said. “It is not enough to make a season. It can make only a minute.”

Mara thought of the grey afternoons she had always disliked, the cold mornings when the world seemed to hold its breath. She had never considered how many lost minutes might be gathered in one life. How many rooms could be built from them.

“Why give it to us?” she asked.

The old woman looked at Elias.

“Because he noticed.”

Elias bent over the clock. Somewhere within its mechanism, a tiny wheel waited for the missing tooth.

Mara opened the window.

The cold entered at once, carrying the smell of chimney smoke and distant pine. She held the vial over the clock’s open face and let the drop fall.

For one second, nothing happened.

Then the clock chimed.

The sound was unlike any bell Mara had heard. It was bright and clear, like water poured into sunlight.

The wheel turned.

The hands moved forward.

And across the street, every leaf remaining on the trees began to unfurl.

When Mara looked back, the old woman had vanished. The clock was gone. The box lay empty on the table.

Only the brass plaque remained, and on it, new words had appeared:

**THE HOUSE AT THE END OF WINTER**  
**Closed until the first lost minute of spring.**

Elias stepped outside. The frost was melting from the pavement in shining ribbons. Somewhere, a bird sang a note so sudden and sweet that both of them jumped.

“You should return to your master,” Mara said.

“Why?”

“For the apprenticeship.”

“I passed,” Elias told her. “That was the last day.”

Mara laughed, though she wasn’t sure why. Perhaps because a missing minute had given a boy his future, or perhaps because the world had nearly been trapped in winter for want of one small, forgotten thing.

She walked him to the end of the street. Behind them, the house creaked, settled, and became ordinary again. Its windows darkened. Its roof looked patched and tired. It was simply a house that had never been opened.

At the corner, Elias turned back.

“Will I see you again?” he asked.

Mara looked up. Though it was still November, the sky above the rooftops was the pale, hopeful blue of March.

“Probably,” she said. “But you may have to wait for a missing minute.”

He nodded and walked away.

Mara returned home and placed a small jar on her windowsill. She filled it with rainwater and labeled it:

**FOR THE FIRST SPRING.**

She did not know why she needed to keep it, but she suspected that some things arrive only once, and if you are not paying attention, they can slip quietly from the world before you ever know their names.
